items.prompt: Under the standard NPV rule, a company should accept an independent project when its NPV is what?

options.label: Less than zero
Greater than zero
Equal to the discount rate
Equal to the initial investment

rubric: A positive NPV means the project adds value after covering the required return.
Distractors confuse NPV with investment size or the discount rate.

items.prompt: In an NPV calculation, which rate is normally used to discount a project's future cash flows?

options.label: The current dividend yield
The project's cost of capital
Last year's inflation rate
The accounting rate of return

rubric: Cash flows are discounted at the required return, i.e. the cost of capital for the project's risk.
Distractors are real rates but not the required return.

items.prompt: What is the internal rate of return (IRR) of a project?

options.label: The interest rate the firm pays its bank
Average yearly profit divided by investment
The discount rate at which NPV equals zero
The discount rate at which payback is one year

rubric: IRR is the rate that sets NPV to zero.
Distractors mix IRR with borrowing cost, accounting return and payback.

items.prompt: Which formula gives net working capital?

options.label: Current assets minus current liabilities
Current assets plus inventory
Cash minus long-term debt
Total assets minus total liabilities

rubric: Net working capital is current assets less current liabilities.
Total assets minus liabilities is equity, not working capital.

items.prompt: Which is a recognised advantage of debt financing compared with equity financing?

options.label: Interest payments are tax-deductible
Lenders share in the firm's profits
Interest is only due when profit is made
Principal never has to be repaid

rubric: Interest creates a tax shield.
Distractors describe features of equity or invent flexibility debt lacks.

items.prompt: Which of the following are components of the cash conversion cycle? Select all that apply.

options.label: Days of dividends declared
Days sales outstanding
Days inventory outstanding
Days payables outstanding

rubric: The cycle is inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days.
Dividend timing is not part of the operating cycle.

items.prompt: A firm requires a 10% return on a new project. Its analyst computes the project's IRR as 14%. Using the standard IRR decision rule for an independent project, what should the firm do?

options.label: Accept, since IRR exceeds the 10% hurdle rate
Reject, since IRR must equal exactly 10%
Accept only if payback is under 14 years
Reject, since IRR is above the cost of capital

rubric: Accept when IRR is greater than the required return.
Distractors reverse the rule or invent a link to payback or equality.

items.prompt: Why is a dollar received today worth more than a dollar received in a year?

options.label: Today's dollar can be invested to earn a return
Inflation always exceeds every interest rate
Future dollars are always taxed at higher rates
Accounting rules value future cash at less

rubric: The time value of money arises from the earning opportunity.
Distractors give false or incidental reasons.

items.prompt: Why is a firm's cost of equity usually higher than its cost of debt?

options.label: Shareholders are paid after lenders, so they bear more risk
Equity holders receive legally fixed payments each year
Dividends are tax-deductible while interest is not
Lenders have a weaker claim on assets than owners

rubric: Equity is residual and riskier, so investors require more.
Distractors reverse the claim priority or tax treatment.

items.prompt: A project has conventional cash flows (an outlay now, inflows later). What happens to its NPV if the discount rate is raised?

options.label: NPV rises
NPV becomes equal to the IRR
NPV is unchanged
NPV falls

rubric: Higher rates shrink the present value of later inflows.
Distractors misread the direction of the discounting effect.

items.prompt: Which of these is best classified as a working capital decision?

options.label: Choosing between two competing machine designs
Deciding to acquire a rival company outright
Issuing ten-year bonds to build a new plant
Setting how long customers have to pay invoices

rubric: Credit terms affect receivables, a current asset.
Others are long-term investment or financing decisions.

items.prompt: Why does NPV analysis use projected cash flows rather than accounting profit?

options.label: Profit includes only the cash a firm spends on capital
Cash flows ignore the size of the investment needed
Accounting profit is always illegal to forecast
Cash flows show when money is actually received or paid

rubric: Value depends on the timing of actual cash, not accruals.
Distractors misdescribe profit and cash flow.

items.prompt: Which statements explain why heavy use of debt raises a firm's financial risk? Select all that apply.

options.label: Failure to pay can push the firm into bankruptcy
Shareholder earnings become more volatile
Interest payments become optional in bad years
Interest must be paid even when profits fall

rubric: Fixed obligations create distress risk and leverage volatility.
Interest is a binding obligation, not optional.

items.prompt: A retailer negotiates with its suppliers to extend payment terms from 30 days to 60 days. Sales and inventory levels stay the same. What is the most likely effect?

options.label: The cash conversion cycle shortens, freeing up cash
Inventory days fall, because suppliers deliver faster
The cash conversion cycle lengthens, tying up cash
Days sales outstanding rises, slowing collection

rubric: Longer payables days shorten the cycle and retain cash longer.
Distractors reverse the direction or confuse other components.

items.prompt: A project has a positive NPV when discounted at the firm's cost of capital. What does this tell you?

options.label: Its IRR is lower than the discount rate being applied to it
It repays the initial outlay in under one year of operation
Its accounting profit is positive in every year of its life
Its returns exceed the cost of capital, so it adds value

rubric: A positive NPV means discounted inflows exceed the outlay, so returns beat the required return.
Distractors confuse NPV with payback speed, accounting profit, or reverse the IRR comparison.

items.prompt: Why do corporate finance models discount future cash flows before comparing them with today's investment?

options.label: Inflation guarantees that every future payment is worth less in real terms
Money available today can be invested to earn a return, so it is worth more
Discounting lowers the total so that fewer projects look attractive overall
Cash received later is always less certain to arrive than cash today

rubric: The time value of money: cash today can earn a return, so earlier cash is worth more.
Distractors cite only risk, only inflation, or a purpose (reducing accepted projects) that is not the rationale.

items.prompt: A company pays 6% interest on its debt and faces a 25% tax rate. Why is its after-tax cost of debt lower than 6%?

options.label: Debt is repaid before equity, so its true cost is always lower than quoted
Interest payments are tax deductible, which reduces the firm's tax bill
Tax authorities refund a share of the principal when a loan is repaid
Lenders charge lower rates to firms that pay corporate income tax

rubric: Interest is deductible, creating a tax shield so after-tax cost is 6% x (1 - 0.25).
Distractors invent lender discounts, repayment-priority effects, or principal refunds.

items.prompt: Which of these is a component of a firm's net working capital?

options.label: Inventory
Common stock
Factory building
Long-term bonds

rubric: Inventory is a current asset and part of working capital.
Other options are long-term assets or long-term financing.

items.prompt: A conventional project has an outlay today followed by positive cash inflows. If the discount rate rises, what happens to its NPV, and why?

options.label: It stays the same, because the cash flows themselves have not changed
It rises, because the initial outlay is discounted more heavily than inflows
It rises, because a higher rate signals the project is more profitable
It falls, because later inflows are discounted more heavily than the outlay

rubric: Higher rates shrink the present value of future inflows while the outlay today is unchanged, so NPV falls.
Distractors treat the rate as a profitability signal or ignore the effect of discounting.

items.prompt: A firm is deciding whether to launch a new product line. Which of the following are relevant cash flows for the decision? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rent the firm gives up by using a vacant building it already owns
A market study fee that was paid last year and cannot be recovered
The extra inventory and receivables the new line will require
Head-office overhead allocated to the line that would be incurred anyway

rubric: Relevant flows are incremental: added working capital and opportunity costs count.
Sunk costs and unchanged allocated overhead do not change with the decision.

items.prompt: A retailer's sales are flat, but its cash conversion cycle has lengthened from 40 days to 60 days over the year. Management asks what this change means for the business.

options.label: Profit margins must have fallen by one third during the year
The retailer is collecting from customers faster than before
The retailer is paying its suppliers sooner, which frees up cash
Cash is tied up in operations for longer, so more financing is needed

rubric: A longer cycle means cash is locked in inventory and receivables for more days, raising funding needs.
Distractors misread the direction of the change or confuse the cycle with margins.

items.prompt: A project costs 1,000 today and returns 600 at the end of year 1 and 600 at the end of year 2. The discount rate is 10%. What is the NPV, to the nearest whole number?
rubric: Distractors ignore discounting (200) or slip on the calculation.

items.prompt: A firm's hurdle rate is 10%. Three independent projects, X, Y and Z, have IRRs of 7%, 11% and 14%, and funds are not limited. Which should it accept?

options.label: X only
Y and Z
X, Y and Z
Z only

rubric: Accept every independent project whose IRR exceeds the hurdle: Y and Z.
Choosing only the highest IRR ignores that funds are unlimited.

items.prompt: A project costs 900 and produces cash flows of 300, 400 and 500 in years 1 to 3, spread evenly within each year. What is its payback period?

options.label: 2.4 years
2.5 years
2.0 years
3.0 years

rubric: Cumulative cash after year 2 is 700; the remaining 200 takes 200/500 = 0.4 of year 3.
Distractors round to whole years or mis-fraction the final year.

items.prompt: A firm is financed 60% by equity costing 10% and 40% by debt with a pre-tax cost of 5%. The tax rate is 20%. What is its WACC?
rubric: After-tax debt cost is 4%; WACC = 0.6 x 10% + 0.4 x 4% = 7.6%.
8.0% comes from forgetting the tax shield on debt.

items.prompt: A firm has year-end receivables of 150,000 and annual credit sales of 1,825,000. Using a 365-day year, what is its days sales outstanding?

options.label: 30 days
50 days
12 days
60 days

rubric: Other values come from inverting the ratio or using the wrong base.

items.prompt: A manufacturer wants to shorten its cash conversion cycle without reducing sales. Which actions would do this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Tighten collection procedures to cut overdue receivables
Negotiate longer payment terms with its main suppliers
Hold a larger safety stock of finished goods
Offer customers 60-day payment terms instead of 30

rubric: Extending payables and collecting receivables faster both shorten the cycle.
Longer customer terms and higher inventory lengthen it.

items.prompt: A manager is evaluating a machine costing 50,000 that will generate after-tax cash flows of 20,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years. The firm's required return is 8%, and the 3-year annuity factor at 8% is 2.577. What should the manager conclude?

options.label: Reject; NPV is about -1,500 because discounted inflows fall short of the outlay
Accept; NPV is about +10,000 because total inflows of 60,000 exceed the outlay
Reject; NPV is zero because the project's IRR equals the 8% required return
Accept; NPV is about +1,500 because discounted inflows exceed the outlay

rubric: PV of inflows = 20,000 x 2.577 = 51,540, so NPV is about +1,540 and the project is accepted.
Distractors ignore discounting, flip the sign, or misstate the IRR.

items.prompt: A project costs $1,000 today and returns $600 at the end of year 1 and $600 at the end of year 2. The discount rate is 10%. What is the NPV?
rubric: $200 ignores discounting; $1,041.32 is the PV of inflows and forgets to subtract the outlay.

items.prompt: A firm is financed 60% by equity and 40% by debt at market values. Cost of equity is 12%, pre-tax cost of debt is 6%, and the tax rate is 25%. What is its WACC?
rubric: 9.6% omits the tax shield; 7.5% swaps the weights.

items.prompt: The risk-free rate is 3%, the expected market return is 8%, and a stock's beta is 1.2. Using CAPM, what is the cost of equity?
rubric: 9.6% multiplies beta by the market return rather than the premium; 6.0% leaves out the risk-free rate.

items.prompt: An investment of $900 returns $300, $400 and $500 at the end of years 1, 2 and 3, spread evenly within each year. What is the payback period?

options.label: 3.0 years
2.8 years
2.2 years
2.4 years

rubric: Cumulative cash is $700 after year 2, so $200 of the $500 in year 3 is needed: 2 + 0.4 = 2.4.
3.0 years rounds up to a whole year; others misplace the fraction.

items.prompt: A distributor holds inventory for 50 days on average, collects receivables in 40 days, and pays suppliers in 30 days. What is its cash conversion cycle?

options.label: 40 days
20 days
60 days
120 days

rubric: CCC = DIO + DSO - DPO = 50 + 40 - 30 = 60 days.
120 days adds payables instead of subtracting them.

items.prompt: Which cash flows belong in the incremental NPV of a new product line? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rent the firm could earn by leasing out the owned warehouse the line will occupy
$50,000 market study already paid last year
Interest payments on the loan used to fund the line
Increase in inventory and receivables needed to support the new line

rubric: Working capital needs and opportunity costs are incremental cash flows.
Sunk costs are irrelevant, and financing costs are captured in the discount rate.

items.prompt: A firm can buy a machine for $50,000. It will save $18,000 a year for 4 years and then have no value. The firm's required return is 20%, and the 4-year annuity factor at 20% is 2.5887. What is the NPV and the decision?

options.label: NPV is about -$3,400, so reject the machine
NPV is about -$33,600, so reject because year 1 savings are below cost
NPV is about +$22,000, so accept because total savings exceed cost
NPV is about +$7,060, so accept the machine

rubric: PV of savings = 18,000 x 2.5887 = 46,597, so NPV = -3,403 and the machine is rejected.
The +$22,000 option ignores discounting; the others misuse the annuity.

items.prompt: Two mutually exclusive projects, cost of capital 10%. A: outlay $100k, IRR 28%, NPV $40k. B: outlay $600k, IRR 19%, NPV $90k. Why do the rankings conflict, and which should be chosen?

options.label: IRR is a percentage and ignores risk, so choose A as the safer project
NPV overstates large projects, so choose A because percentage returns compare fairly
They differ in scale; B adds more value in dollars, so choose B
A's higher IRR means more value per dollar, so it adds more value; choose A

rubric: For mutually exclusive projects, NPV measures the dollar value added; IRR ignores scale.
Choosing A ignores the larger absolute value B creates.

items.prompt: A firm's WACC uses the 4% coupon on its old bonds as the cost of debt, though comparable new bonds would yield 7%. What is the effect of this choice?

options.label: Cost of debt is correct because the coupon is what the firm contractually pays, so WACC is accurate
Cost of debt is understated because financing is priced at current yields, so WACC is too low and weak projects may pass
Cost of debt is irrelevant because only equity cost drives WACC, so WACC is unchanged
Cost of debt is overstated because older coupons already include the tax shield, so WACC is too high

rubric: The relevant cost is the current marginal market yield, not historical coupons.
Using 4% understates the hurdle rate and risks accepting value-destroying projects.

items.prompt: A firm swaps 20% of its equity for debt. EPS rises, yet its share price barely changes. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: Remaining shareholders bear more financial risk, so required equity return rises and offsets the cheaper debt
Higher EPS always raises price, so the market must be mispricing the shares
Share count fell, so EPS rose because earnings grew, and price lags earnings
Debt has no tax benefit in this case, so only EPS is affected

rubric: Leverage raises equity risk and the cost of equity, offsetting the gain from cheaper debt apart from the tax shield.
EPS growth from leverage is not value creation by itself.

items.prompt: A profitable firm grows sales 30% and runs short of cash. Net income rose, receivables and inventory each rose 40%, and payables rose 5%. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The firm holds too much equity and should issue debt to fix liquidity
The rise in receivables shows sales are fictitious and profit is not real
Growth is absorbing cash in receivables and inventory faster than supplier credit funds it
Net income is overstated because depreciation was added back

rubric: Rapid growth ties up cash in working capital that payables only partly finance.
Profit and cash differ; nothing indicates fraud or depreciation errors.

items.prompt: An analyst forecasts cash flows that grow with inflation (nominal) but discounts them at a 6% real rate, with expected inflation of 3%. What is the likely consequence?

options.label: NPV is overstated, because nominal flows are discounted at too low a rate
NPV is understated, because real rates are always lower than nominal rates
NPV is unaffected, because the rate only matters for the terminal value
NPV is unaffected, because inflation cancels out across years

rubric: Nominal flows need a nominal rate (about 9%); using the real rate overstates present values.
Inflation does not cancel when flows and rate are inconsistent.

items.prompt: An analyst discounts a project's cash flows at WACC. Which of the items in the cash flows are errors? Select all that apply.

options.label: Depreciation added back to after-tax operating profit
Allocated head-office overhead that will not change if the project is accepted
Interest expense on the project's debt deducted from cash flows
Tax computed on operating profit after depreciation

rubric: Interest is already captured in WACC, so deducting it double counts; unchanged allocated overhead is not incremental.
Adding back depreciation and taxing after depreciation are standard.

items.prompt: A firm with a 10% cost of capital must pick one of two repeatable machines. Machine A lasts 3 years with NPV $100k; machine B lasts 6 years with NPV $150k. Which reasoning is best?

options.label: Choose A, because its equivalent annual annuity (about $40k) beats B's (about $34k) when both can be repeated
Choose B, because its higher NPV means more total value regardless of life
Choose B, because a longer life gives more total cash and so is always safer
Treat them as equal, because both have positive NPV and either adds value

rubric: With unequal lives and replacement, compare equivalent annual annuities: 100/2.487 is about 40 versus 150/4.355 is about 34.
Comparing raw NPVs ignores the different durations.

items.prompt: Project A has an IRR of 25% and an NPV of 10M at the firm's 10% cost of capital. Project B, which is mutually exclusive with A and larger, has an IRR of 18% and an NPV of 30M. Which analysis best explains why the two criteria rank them differently?

options.label: IRR is computed on pre-tax flows, while NPV uses after-tax flows, which changes the ranking
IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself and ignores project scale, while NPV uses the cost of capital
NPV depends on accounting profit, while IRR depends on cash flow, so the rankings diverge
NPV ignores when cash flows arrive, while IRR discounts them, so the two cannot agree on timing

rubric: IRR is a percentage that ignores scale and implicitly reinvests interim flows at the IRR; NPV is in value terms at the cost of capital.
Distractors misstate how NPV and IRR treat timing, taxes and accounting profit; both use after-tax cash flows and discount timing.

items.prompt: A project has cash flows of -100 at time 0, +260 at time 1 and -165 at time 2. A spreadsheet finds IRRs of both 10% and 50%. What explains this result?

options.label: The cash flows change sign twice, so the NPV equation can have two roots
The spreadsheet rounds the discount rate, which creates a duplicate solution near the true IRR
The total outflows exceed the inflows, so the IRR is undefined and the software guesses
The large second-period inflow doubles the effective discount rate used in the iteration

rubric: Two sign changes in the cash flows allow up to two IRRs, so IRR is unreliable for non-conventional flows.
Distractors treat the result as a software artefact or a size effect rather than a property of the sign pattern.

items.prompt: In a no-tax setting, a firm swaps 30% of its equity for debt and its WACC stays almost unchanged, even though debt is cheaper than equity. Which analysis best explains this?

options.label: Debt's cost rises to match equity's as soon as any borrowing occurs, so the weights no longer matter
WACC weights are set from book values, which do not change when a recapitalisation occurs
Investors disregard debt when valuing operating assets, so the firm's discount rate stays fixed
Shareholders face riskier residual cash flows, so the cost of equity rises enough to offset the cheaper debt

rubric: Higher leverage raises equity risk and the required return on equity, offsetting the cheaper debt in the WACC.
Distractors invent mechanisms about debt cost, book weights or investor neglect that do not match the leverage-risk relationship.

items.prompt: A distributor's sales rose from 100M to 120M, and its year-end receivables rose from 12M to 21.8M. Using a 365-day year, which diagnosis best fits these figures?

options.label: Customers are paying faster, and the larger balance reflects bigger orders at year end
Collection slowed, with days sales outstanding rising from about 44 to about 66 days
Inventory turnover has slowed, which is what the larger receivables balance reflects
Growth explains it, since receivables should rise far faster than sales in an expanding firm

rubric: DSO = receivables/sales x 365 rose from about 44 to about 66 days, which points to looser credit terms or weaker collection.
Distractors attribute the change to growth, faster payment or inventory, none of which the DSO calculation supports.

items.prompt: A project has a base-case NPV of +20M. A 10% fall in selling price lowers NPV by 25M, a 10% rise in unit cost lowers it by 4M, and a 10% fall in volume lowers it by 9M. Which variable's forecast error is the key risk to the accept decision?

options.label: All three equally, because each reduces NPV when forecasts miss
Unit cost, because costs are the largest line and the cheapest to misjudge
Selling price, because a 10% miss alone turns the NPV negative
Volume, because it drives both revenue and variable cost at once

rubric: Only the price shock pushes NPV below zero (20 - 25 = -5), so it determines the decision.
Distractors ignore the magnitudes: the cost and volume shocks leave NPV positive, and the sensitivities are not equal.

items.prompt: A firm is estimating incremental after-tax cash flows for a new product line that will be discounted at WACC. Which items should be excluded from those cash flows? Select all that apply.

options.label: The 1.5M consultant fee already paid for the feasibility study
Corporate head-office overhead allocated to the line that will not change if it is launched
Interest on the loan raised to fund the launch, since financing is captured in the discount rate
Lost contribution from an existing product that the new line will cannibalise

rubric: Sunk costs, unchanged allocated overhead and financing charges are not incremental project cash flows.
Cannibalised contribution is a real incremental loss and must be included; excluding it is the common error.

items.prompt: A firm with an 8% WACC is appraising a venture in a new, volatile market. Comparable firms in that market imply a risk-appropriate rate of 14%. The analyst reports NPV +6M at 8% and tells the board the project is value-creating. At 14% the NPV is -9M. What is the root error in the analyst's work?

options.label: The firm-wide WACC was applied to a project with a different risk profile, overstating its value
The NPV should have been replaced by payback because the market is volatile
The 14% rate should be averaged with 8% because both are valid estimates of project risk
Cash flows should have been forecast after interest so the 8% rate matched them

rubric: Discount rates should reflect the project's systematic risk, not the firm's average; at the right rate the NPV is negative.
Distractors misplace the issue in cash flow definition, method choice or averaging rates, which does not fix the risk mismatch.

items.prompt: Two mutually exclusive machines each meet an ongoing need that will be replaced like-for-like. Machine X lasts 3 years with NPV 24k, and Machine Y lasts 6 years with NPV 38k, both at the same 10% rate. Criteria: maximise value per year of service when replacement is repeated. Which approach is best?

options.label: Pick whichever has the higher IRR, since IRR removes the effect of project life
Pick Y because its NPV is higher and NPV always decides between exclusive projects
Pick X because shorter projects carry less forecast risk and recover their cost sooner
Compare equivalent annual annuities, since the lives differ and replacement will repeat

rubric: With unequal lives and repeated replacement, equivalent annual annuity (or a replacement chain) puts the projects on a common basis.
Raw NPV ignores the different lives, and the IRR and risk arguments do not solve the comparison.

items.prompt: A firm has a 100M budget limit this year and cannot carry funds forward. Project A costs 60M with NPV 18M, B costs 40M with NPV 14M, and C costs 50M with NPV 15M. Projects are indivisible. Criterion: maximise total NPV. Which choice is best?

options.label: B and C, total NPV 29M
A and C, total NPV 33M
A and B, total NPV 32M
A only, total NPV 18M

rubric: A+B costs exactly 100M and gives NPV 32M, the best feasible combination.
A+C costs 110M and is infeasible; B+C is feasible but lower, and choosing by highest PI alone misses the best combination.

items.prompt: A young firm has volatile cash flows, mostly intangible assets and large growth options, and needs 50M. Criteria: minimise expected financial distress costs and preserve flexibility to invest. Which financing is best justified?

options.label: Debt, because the interest tax shield is worth more than any expected distress costs
Equity, because it has no cost to the firm so long as no dividend is declared
Equity, because intangible assets give weak collateral and fixed payments risk distress
Debt, because lenders will price in the growth options and offer cheap rates

rubric: Trade-off theory favours low leverage for firms with volatile cash flows, intangible assets and growth options.
Distractors overstate the tax shield or claim equity is free, ignoring the required return shareholders demand.

items.prompt: A supplier offers terms of 2/10 net 30 on a 100k invoice. The firm's credit line costs 9% a year. Criterion: minimise annual financing cost. Using a 365-day year, which action is best?

options.label: Pay on day 30, since the 2% discount is small next to the cost of drawing on the credit line
Pay on day 10 only if cash is on hand, since borrowing to take the discount is too risky
Pay on day 30, since delaying payment is free credit and cheaper than any bank borrowing
Pay on day 10 using the credit line, as the discount implies an annual rate near 37%

rubric: Skipping the discount costs about 2/98 x 365/20 = roughly 37% annualised, far above the 9% credit line.
Distractors treat trade credit as free or the discount as trivial, ignoring the implied annual rate.

items.prompt: A board wants to use a 3-year payback rule for a drug-development project with heavy early costs and large cash flows from year 5 onward. Which critique of the rule is most valid?

options.label: It ignores cash flows after the cutoff and time value, so it may reject a positive-NPV project
It uses accounting profit instead of cash flow, which understates the project's early returns
It favours long projects, so it will accept projects whose value is below their cost
It requires a cost of capital estimate, which is unavailable for risky development projects

rubric: Payback ignores cash flows beyond the cutoff and the time value of money, which biases against long-dated value.
Distractors misdescribe payback: it uses cash flows, needs no discount rate, and biases toward short projects.

items.prompt: A manager proposes ranking all of the firm's projects, including mutually exclusive ones, by IRR alone. Which are valid criticisms of this proposal? Select all that apply.

options.label: IRR cannot be calculated for any project that has a positive NPV at the cost of capital
A higher IRR can belong to a smaller project with lower value added than a larger one
IRR implicitly assumes interim cash flows are reinvested at the IRR itself
Unconventional cash flows can produce several IRRs, making the figure ambiguous

rubric: Multiple roots, scale blindness and the reinvestment assumption are the standard weaknesses of IRR as a sole ranking criterion.
IRR is usually computable for positive-NPV projects, so the last claim is false.

items.prompt: A cyclical manufacturer has 200M of debt at 6%, so interest is 12M. EBIT is about 80M normally but fell to 45M in the last downturn. Its loan covenant requires EBIT/interest of at least 3x. Criteria: capture some tax shield while staying compliant even in a downturn with a margin. Which plan is best?

options.label: Add 30M of debt, keeping downturn coverage above 3x with a small safety margin
Add 100M of debt for a buyback, since normal-year coverage would stay above 4x
Add 200M of debt to maximise the shield, since normal-year coverage stays above 3x
Add no debt, since any tax shield is outweighed by distress costs for a cyclical firm

rubric: Adding 30M gives interest of 13.8M and downturn coverage of about 3.3x, so it stays compliant with a margin.
Adding 100M gives downturn coverage of 2.5x and adding 200M gives about 1.9x, both breaching the covenant; zero debt gives up value without need.

items.prompt: Two mutually exclusive projects have the same risk, and the cost of capital is 10%. Project A has IRR 25% and NPV 40k. Project B has IRR 18% and NPV 70k. Judged by the goal of maximising shareholder value, which choice is best?

options.label: Choose either, because both clear the 10% hurdle and both create positive value
Choose A, because IRR does not depend on the discount rate and is more reliable
Choose A, because its higher IRR shows more return per dollar and so lower risk
Choose B, because NPV measures the absolute value added and IRR ignores project scale

rubric: NPV gives the dollar value added, which is what matters for mutually exclusive projects of different scale.
Distractors treat IRR as a risk or reliability measure or ignore that capital is used for only one project.

items.prompt: A conglomerate discounts every division's projects at one firm-wide WACC of 9%. Its utility division is low-risk and its biotech division is high-risk. Which critique of this policy is most valid?

options.label: It is fine, because WACC is set by the firm's financing mix and not by the assets invested in
It favours high-risk projects and rejects safe ones, so rates should reflect each project's own risk
It is fine, because diversification across divisions removes the risk differences between projects
It overstates value for safe divisions, so it should use the lowest division's rate everywhere

rubric: A single rate over-accepts risky projects and under-accepts safe ones; rates should follow project risk, for example pure-play betas.
Distractors confuse financing mix with asset risk or assume diversification justifies one rate.

items.prompt: A CFO argues: "Debt costs 5% and equity costs 12%, so raising the debt share keeps lowering WACC, and we should lever up as far as lenders allow." Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Flawed, because cost of equity rises with leverage, and distress costs eventually offset the tax shield
Correct, because the interest tax shield grows with debt and nothing else changes as leverage rises
Flawed, because debt is always costlier than equity once default risk is priced into the bond yield
Correct, because lenders will cap leverage at the level that is optimal for shareholders anyway

rubric: Equity holders demand more return as leverage rises, and distress costs offset the tax shield, so the optimum is interior.
Distractors assume a free lunch from debt or claim debt is always costlier than equity.

items.prompt: A supplier offers terms of 2/10 net 30. The firm has a bank credit line at 9% annual interest. Judged on cost of financing alone, which policy is best?

options.label: Take the discount only when cash is idle, since borrowing to pay early adds risk
Take the discount using the line, because forgoing it implies about 37% annualised borrowing cost
Pay on day 30, because a 2% discount is too small to matter next to interest costs
Pay on day 30 always, because trade credit is free financing and the bank line is dearer

rubric: Forgoing 2% to delay 20 days costs about (2/98)*(365/20), roughly 37% a year, far above 9%.
Distractors treat the discount as small or the credit as free, ignoring annualisation.

items.prompt: A DCF values a firm with a 5% perpetual terminal growth rate. Long-run nominal GDP growth is about 3.5%, and terminal value is 80% of the total value. Which judgement is most defensible?

options.label: The 5% is acceptable, because terminal value share matters less than explicit-period forecasts
The 5% is too high, since it implies eventually exceeding the economy, so cap it near 3.5% and test sensitivity
The 5% is acceptable, because strong firms can always outgrow the economy as a whole
The terminal value should be dropped, because anything beyond the forecast horizon is speculative

rubric: Perpetual growth above the economy's growth is not sustainable and is magnified when terminal value dominates.
Distractors defend the high rate or discard terminal value entirely.

items.prompt: A project has cash flows of -100 at t0, +260 at t1 and -165 at t2. Its IRRs are 10% and 50%. Which judgements are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Average the two IRRs to get 30% and compare that with the hurdle rate
Accept whenever any one IRR exceeds the cost of capital, since it signals a positive return
The project has multiple IRRs, so IRR alone cannot give a reliable accept or reject signal
A modified IRR, which reinvests at the cost of capital, gives one rate and avoids the ambiguity
Compute NPV at the cost of capital, because it stays well defined with sign changes

rubric: Two sign changes produce multiple IRRs; NPV and MIRR remain unambiguous.
Distractors use an arbitrary IRR or an average that has no economic meaning.

items.prompt: A firm needs 40m for a high-return expansion. Net debt/EBITDA is 1.5x against a covenant of 4x, and cash flows are stable. Management believes its shares are undervalued by the market. Judged on cost and signalling, which financing choice is best?

options.label: Issue debt, since ample capacity avoids selling undervalued shares and an equity issue would signal overvaluation
Issue equity, since stable cash flows mean the market will price new shares fairly
Split evenly, since a mix is always best regardless of capacity, valuation and signalling
Issue new equity, since it avoids covenant risk and preserves flexibility for later growth

rubric: With low leverage and stable cash flows, debt avoids dilution at a low price and the negative signal of an equity issue.
Distractors ignore the undervaluation and signalling criteria or default to a mix.

items.prompt: A firm will build a 10-year plant earning euro revenues. It wants financing that avoids refinancing and currency mismatch. Which design best meets both constraints?

options.label: Issue a 10-year dollar bond and leave it unhedged to keep the coupon lower
Issue a 10-year fixed-rate euro bond so liabilities match the asset's life and currency
Roll a 1-year dollar credit line each year because short-term rates are lower
Issue a 3-year euro bond and refinance later, since the term premium is smaller

rubric: Matching maturity and currency removes refinancing and FX risk.
Distractors save on coupon but create refinancing or currency mismatch.

items.prompt: An analyst's model forecasts cash flows in real terms, with no inflation, but discounts them at a nominal WACC of 9%. What is the essential fix?

options.label: Keep the model, because real cash flows are always safer to discount at a higher rate
Add inflation to the discount rate again, to be conservative about risk
Use a consistent basis: nominal flows at the nominal rate, or real flows at a real rate
Remove WACC and use the risk-free rate, because inflation is already in real flows

rubric: Cash flows and the discount rate must both be nominal or both be real; mixing understates value.
Distractors treat the mismatch as conservatism or swap in an unrelated rate.

items.prompt: A pilot-able project has a standalone NPV of -5m, but if a 2m pilot succeeds a 40m expansion becomes worth +12m NPV, with a 40% chance of success. The firm wants to keep downside limited. Which plan works best?

options.label: Reject outright, since the standalone NPV is negative and so no plan can add value
Wait several years, since delay always raises the value of an uncertain project
Commit the full investment now, so the firm captures the expansion with certainty
Fund the 2m pilot and expand only if it succeeds, valuing the staged option as positive

rubric: Staging caps the loss at 2m and keeps the upside: 0.4*12 = 4.8m expected, against a 2m cost.
Distractors ignore the option value or add commitment risk.

items.prompt: Pure-play comparables have equity beta 1.2 and D/E 0.5, with a 20% tax rate. A division will be financed at D/E 0.25. Using Hamada's formula, what equity beta should be used for the division?
rubric: Distractors skip a step or use the wrong direction.

items.prompt: A 10m budget is fixed and projects are indivisible. A: cost 6, NPV 3.0. B: cost 4, NPV 2.5. C: cost 5, NPV 2.6. D: cost 5, NPV 2.0. Which selection maximises total NPV?

options.label: B and C, found by ranking on profitability index
B and D, ranked by cost
C and D, using the full budget
A and B, using the full budget

rubric: A+B gives NPV 5.5, above B+C at 5.1; greedy PI ranking fails with indivisible projects and leftover budget.
Distractors use PI ranking or other combinations that yield lower NPV.

items.prompt: A new-product NPV, discounted at WACC, includes only incremental sales and operating costs. Which items must be added for the analysis to be correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Lost profits on the firm's existing product that the new one will cannibalise
The initial working capital investment and its recovery at the end
The opportunity cost of an idle warehouse the project will use instead of renting it out
Interest expense on the debt used, deducted from the project cash flows each year
The 3m already spent on R&D, since it was caused by this product

rubric: Incremental cash flows include cannibalisation, working capital and opportunity costs.
Interest is captured in WACC and sunk R&D is irrelevant, so including them is wrong.

items.prompt: A firm needs 50m. EBITDA is 100m and net debt is 200m. Its policy is to keep net debt/EBITDA at or below 2.5x with at least 0.25x headroom, and not to issue equity below intrinsic value. It also plans a 30m annual buyback. Which plan meets every constraint?

options.label: Borrow 40m and issue 10m of equity, reaching 2.4x with a small dilution
Borrow 25m and suspend 25m of buybacks, ending at 2.25x with no equity issue
Issue 50m of new equity, keeping leverage at 2.0x and the headroom intact
Borrow 50m, reaching 2.5x, because the policy ceiling is met exactly

rubric: Borrowing 25m gives 225/100 = 2.25x, within the headroom rule, and buyback cash covers the rest with no equity issue.
Distractors breach the headroom rule or the no-issue constraint.
